title: The point shortcut
scenario: A new harbor: the ferry company wants the fewest stops from the pier to the lighthouse. The bay road looks direct — but is it the shortest?

intro.job: A new harbor: the ferry company wants the fewest stops from the pier to the lighthouse. The bay road looks direct — but is it the shortest?

idea.rule: A queue walks outward in rings — the first time you reach a stop is the fewest stops to it.
idea.detail: Same question as Fewest stops, new harbor. A depth-first walk takes the first road out of the pier — the bay — and follows it all the way, so the first way it finds can be the long way round. Walk outward in rings instead: a queue holds the stops still to visit, nearest first. Take a stop off the front, put its unseen neighbours on the back with one more stop, and mark them seen right away. The first time the target comes off the queue, its count is the fewest stops.

model_restatement: Say how many stops the shortest trip from the start stop to the target stop takes.

clarify.question: Do you want the fewest stops, or just any way there?
clarify.answer: The fewest stops — the shortest trip, counted in stops.

clarify.question: Does the order I visit stops in matter — should I use a queue?
clarify.answer: Yes. A queue visits stops in rings, nearest first, so the first time you reach the target is the fewest stops.

clarify.question: What if there's no way to reach the target?
Can the walk come to the same stop twice — should I revisit it?
clarify.answer: Never revisit. The first time you reach a stop is already its fewest stops, so mark it seen right then.

clarify_fallback: Good question — assume the simple case.
blueprint: Walk from the start, take each route out and go as deep as it leads, counting stops. The first time you reach the target, return the count.

checkpoints.prompt: The first call reaches line 2. Which stop is node?
The walk takes its first route. On the next call, which stop is node?
With the fix — the second stop comes off the front of the queue. Which stop is node?

why_line: The draft walks deep first: pier → bay → dock → lighthouse is 3 stops — but the point shortcut (pier → point → lighthouse) is 2. Depth-first returns the first way it finds, not the fewest.

explain.rule: A depth-first walk is a driver who takes the first turn at every junction and only turns back at a dead end — the first way it finds isn't the shortest.
explain.bridge: The walk goes pier → bay → dock → lighthouse. What would it have to do to try the point road before going that deep?

fix.rule: Walk outward in rings with a queue: take stops off the front, put new ones on the back one stop further out, and mark each stop seen when you first reach it.

walk.gloss: The start is seen before anything else.
Take the nearest stop off the front of the queue.
Mark a stop seen the moment it's first reached — that's its fewest stops.
New stops go on the back, one stop further out.

alternatives.note: The same rings with a plain list: pop(0) takes from the front. Fine for small maps; deque.popleft() is the fast way.

hints: Follow the draft from the pier. Which road does it take first — and does it ever try the point?
Depth-first returns the first way it finds, not the one with the fewest stops.
Use a queue: deque([(start, 0)]), popleft() the nearest stop, and append each unseen neighbour with stops + 1, marking it seen.

follow_up.prompt: The dock road is rebuilt — same map, dock goes to the beacon, beacon to the light. Fewest stops from the pier to the light now?

checkpoint.prompt: With the dock going to the beacon, what gets printed?

follow_up.fix_hint: The point road still wins: pier → point → light is 2 stops; the draft's deep walk takes 4.

one_liner: A queue walks outward in rings — the first time you reach a stop is the fewest stops to it.
